turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You think you can easily dismiss Mr. Wickham's misfortunes, but I know the truth of his character, and I will not let you pretend otherwise.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, my dear Elizabeth, that I am astonished by your obstinacy and your refusal to see the good in me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You are astonished by my obstinacy? I should think it more astonishing if I were to ignore the evidence of your own behavior and pretend that you are worthy of my regard.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am not surprised, Elizabeth, that you would so readily believe the worst of me, given your own prejudices and misconceptions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You dare to call my prejudices and misconceptions? I have every reason in the world to think ill of you, and it is not my obstinacy that prevents me from accepting your proposal, but my honest opinion of your character.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you are not in a position to judge my character, Elizabeth. Your own behavior and prejudices have consistently demonstrated a lack of discernment and a tendency to leap to conclusions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be lectured by you on discernment and judgment, sir. Your own behavior has been a constant reminder of the dangers of unguided pride and a lack of consideration for others. You are not in a position to teach me anything.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that your continued refusal to acknowledge my good qualities is a significant obstacle to my hopes for our future together.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am astonished that you can still persist in believing that I am in any way responsible for your own failures and shortcomings. Your arrogance and self-delusion know no bounds, sir.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must say, Elizabeth, that your refusal to acknowledge my good qualities is a reflection of your own limited understanding and capacity for discernment.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How can you continue to pretend that your behavior has been in any way admirable, when it has been a constant source of pain and offense to me and those I care about?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you reconsider your opinion of me, Elizabeth. Your judgment, it seems, is often swayed by emotion rather than reason.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not sure what you find so difficult to understand, Mr. Darcy. Your actions have consistently shown a lack of respect for those you consider to be beneath you, and I have no intention of becoming a part of that pattern.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that I find your continued refusal to accept my affection to be a puzzle, one that I can only attribute to your own prejudices and misconceptions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am astonished that you can be so obtuse, Mr. Darcy, as to think that my refusal is due to any personal failing on my part, when it is so clearly a reaction to your own behavior.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I fear, Elizabeth, that your vehemence in this matter is a testament to your own passion and imagination, rather than any genuine concern for my character or actions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am astonished that you can be so obtuse, Mr. Darcy, as to think that my refusal is due to any personal failing on my part, when it is so clearly a reaction to your own behavior, which you have thus far shown no inclination to change or acknowledge.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Elizabeth, that you are mistaken in your assessment of my character and actions. I have done nothing but what I believed was right, and I will not be lectured on my conduct by one who has so often condemned me without foundation.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be lectured on my conduct by one who has been the principal, if not the only means, of dividing my sister from her husband, and exposing them both to the censure of the world.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that I find it singularly vexing to be rebuffed by one who has so long professed to despise me, while at the same time availing herself of my family's connections and protection.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
